title: Quantum Topological Data Analysis Beyond Betti Numbers: Complexity Hardness $\&$ An Algorithm for Torsion Witness
authors: Nhat A. Nghiem, Dominic W. Berry, Trung V. Phan
abstract: Recent advances have revealed an interplay between quantum computing and topological data analysis (TDA). Most quantum TDA has focused on Betti numbers, which characterize the connectivity and ``holes'' of a dataset. Homology, however, contains additional information in the form of torsion: a nontrivial cycle can become trivial after being repeated finitely, revealing global constraints on how cycles combine and wrap around one another. Beyond applications in biomolecular studies, torsion appears in physical settings including homological quantum rotor codes, discrete charges, and gauge sectors. We study torsion from both classical and quantum perspectives. Given a graph $G$ and its clique complex $K = \mathrm{Cl}(G)$, we first prove that, for fixed $r$ and prime $p$, deciding whether $H_r(K,\mathbb{Z})$ contains $p$-torsion is NP-hard. As a corollary, when a homological rotor code is specified by $G$, deciding whether the code has a finite-dimensional logical sector of a given order is NP-hard. We discuss related problems, including the Bockstein homomorphism, Smith normal form, lattice saturation, and cohomology. Second, for a finite set of primes $P$, we develop a quantum algorithm that serves as a one-sided torsion witness. For fixed $r$, it outputs WITNESS or INCONCLUSIVE, i.e. WITNESS certifies that either $H_r(K,\mathbb{Z})$ or $H_{r-1}(K,\mathbb{Z})$ contains $p$-torsion for some $p\in P$ while INCONCLUSIVE makes no claim about its presence or absence. We identify a regime in which the algorithm achieves a near-quadratic quantum speedup over the corresponding classical algorithm under the same input model. Our NP-hardness result complements recent hardness results for estimating Betti numbers, adding a complexity-theoretic perspective to quantum TDA. Together, these results demonstrate that integral homology, beyond its Betti numbers, can be computationally challenging.
summary: This paper advances quantum TDA by moving beyond simple connectivity measures (Betti numbers) to analyze the computationally difficult torsion structure of homology groups. It proves this detection problem is NP-hard and presents a quantum algorithm that achieves a near-quadratic speedup for detecting this crucial, discrete topological information.
main_problem: The paper investigates extending Topological Data Analysis (TDA) from Betti numbers to include the full integral homology structure, specifically the torsion subgroup, which captures global constraints.
main_result: It proves that determining the presence of $p$-torsion in the homology group is NP-hard, and develops a quantum algorithm achieving a near-quadratic speedup to witness this torsion.
method: The work combines complexity theory (NP-hardness proofs via reduction) with quantum algorithm design, utilizing techniques like the Quantum Singular Value Transformation (QSVT) framework.
model_or_system: The mathematical model is a simplicial complex $K$ derived from a graph $G$, whose homology groups $H_r(K, \mathbb{Z})$ are analyzed. Physical relevance is drawn from homological quantum rotor codes and gauge theory.
key_observables: Betti numbers ($ eta_r$) and the torsion subgroup ($	ext{Tor}_r(K, \mathbb{Z})$), which quantifies discrete topological information.
important_parameters: The prime $p$ and the set of primes $P$ used in the quantum algorithm are key parameters. The complexity analysis depends on the size of the complex and the number of primes.
main_assumptions: The quantum algorithm provides a one-sided witness (WITNESS or INCONCLUSIVE) and does not fully determine the torsion structure, only its presence for specific primes.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the difference between torsion-free and torsion-bearing manifolds (e.g., Annulus vs. Klein bottle) in the context of homology classes.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the NP-hardness of detecting $p$-torsion in homology groups. It then develops a quantum algorithm to act as a one-sided torsion witness, followed by detailed mathematical sections on finite field arithmetic and reversible quantum circuit construction.
why_interesting: The connection between algebraic topology (homology/torsion) and computational complexity, coupled with a quantum speedup claim, provides a new, hard-to-compute diagnostic tool for quantum systems.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Torsion-free and torsion-bearing manifolds. Torsion is detected in the homology classes of closed cycles. (A) An annulus with a noncontractible Z-cycle. (B) A Klein bottle with a Z-cycle and a Z2-cycle γ. Although γ is homologically nontrivial, traversing it twice yields a cycle homologous to zero. The fundamental polygon on the right shows the edge identifications responsible for this Z2-torsion.
